entries.title: 5,000 Classic Movie Posters Digitized & Put Online: Free to Browse & Download
entries.summary: Who hasn’t pinned one of Saul Bass’ elegant film posters on their wall—either with thumbtacks above the dorm room bed or in frame and glass in grown-up environs? Or maybe it’s 70s kitsch you prefer—the art of the grindhouse and sensationalist drive-in exploitation film? Or 20s silent avant-garde, the cool noir of the 30s and […]
entries.content:
Who hasn’t pinned one of Saul Bass’ ele­gant film posters on their wall—either with thumb­tacks above the dorm room bed or in frame and glass in grown-up envi­rons? Or maybe it’s 70s kitsch you prefer—the art of the grind­house and sen­sa­tion­al­ist dri­ve-in exploita­tion film? Or 20s silent avant-garde, the cool noir of the 30s and 40s, 50s B‑grade sci-fi, 60s psy­che­delia and French New Wave, or 80s pop­corn flicks…? What­ev­er kind of cin­e­ma grabs your atten­tion prob­a­bly first grabbed your atten­tion through the design of the movie poster, a genre that gets its due in nov­el­ty shops and spe­cial­ist exhi­bi­tions, but often goes unher­ald­ed in pop­u­lar con­cep­tions of art.

Despite its util­i­tar­i­an and unabashed­ly com­mer­cial func­tion, the movie poster can just as well be a work of art as any oth­er form. Fail­ing that, movie posters are at least always essen­tial archival arti­facts, snap­shots of the weird col­lec­tive uncon­scious of mass cul­ture: from Saul and Elaine Bass’ min­i­mal­ist poster for West Side Sto­ry (1961), “with its bright orange-red back­ground over the title with a sil­hou­ette of a fire escape with dancers” to more com­plex tableaux, like the bald­ly neo-impe­ri­al­ist Africa Texas Style! (1967), “which fea­tures a real­is­tic image of the pro­tag­o­nist on a horse, las­so­ing a zebra in front of a stam­pede of wilde­beest, ele­phants, and giraffes.”

These two descrip­tions only hint at the range of posters archived at the Uni­ver­si­ty of Texas Har­ry Ran­som Cen­ter—upwards of 5,000 in all, “from when the film indus­try was just begin­ning to com­pete with vaude­ville acts in the 1920s to the rise of the mod­ern megaplex and dri­ve-in the­aters in the 1970s.” So wrote Erin Willard in the Ran­som Center’s 2018 announce­ment of the dig­i­ti­za­tion of its mas­sive col­lec­tion. Thou­sands of posters have been pho­tographed and are avail­able online, down­load­able in “Large” and “Extra Large” res­o­lu­tions.

The bulk of the col­lec­tion comes from the Inter­state The­ater Circuit—a chain that, at one time, “con­sist­ed of almost every movie the­ater in Texas”—and encom­pass­es not only posters but film stills, lob­by cards, and press books from “the 1940s through the 1970s with a par­tic­u­lar strength in the films of the 1950s and 60s, includ­ing musi­cals, epics, west­erns, sword and san­dal, hor­ror, and counter cul­ture films.” Oth­er indi­vid­ual col­lec­tors have made siz­able dona­tions of their posters to the cen­ter, and the result is a tour of the many spec­ta­cles avail­able to the mid-cen­tu­ry Amer­i­can mind: lurid, vio­lent excess­es, maudlin mor­al­iz­ing, bizarre erot­ic fan­tasies, dime-store ado­les­cent adven­tures.…

Some of the films are well-known exam­ples from the peri­od; most of them are not, and there­in lies the thrill of brows­ing this online repos­i­to­ry, dis­cov­er­ing obscure odd­i­ties like the 1956 film Bare­foot Bat­tal­ion, in which “teen-age wolf packs become heroes in a nation’s fight for free­dom!” The num­ber of quirks and kinks on dis­play offers us a pruri­ent view of a decade too often flat­ly char­ac­ter­ized by its pen­chant for gray flan­nel suits. The Mad Men era was a peri­od of insti­tu­tion­al repres­sion and ram­pant sex­u­al harass­ment, not unlike our own time. It was also a lab­o­ra­to­ry for a libidi­nous anar­chy that threat­ened to unleash the pent-up ener­gy and cul­tur­al anx­i­ety of mil­lions of frus­trat­ed teenagers onto the world at large, as would hap­pen in the decades to come.

What we see in the mar­ket­ing of films like Five Brand­ed Women (1960) will vary wide­ly depend­ing on our ori­en­ta­tions and polit­i­cal sen­si­bil­i­ties. Is this cheap exploita­tion or an empow­er­ing pre­cur­sor to Mad Max: Fury Road? Maybe both. For cul­tur­al the­o­rists and film his­to­ri­ans, these pulpy adver­tise­ments offer win­dows into the psy­ches of their audi­ences and the film­mak­ers and pro­duc­tion com­pa­nies who gave them what they sup­pos­ed­ly want­ed. For the ordi­nary film buff, the Ran­som Cen­ter col­lec­tion offers eye can­dy of all sorts, and if they hap­pen to own a high-qual­i­ty print­er, the chance to hang posters on their wall that they prob­a­bly won’t see any­where else. Enter the online col­lec­tion here.

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

entries.title: The Genius of Airplane!: How to Make a Comedy by Playing Everything Completely Straight
entries.summary: Not every 46-year-old comedy still gets laughs, but Airplane! seems only to get funnier with the decades. Some viewers too young to have caught it in its theatrical release even take the Benjaminian view of it as the kind of great work that creates its own genre: the rapid-fire deadpan joke machine, we could call it. […]
entries.content:
Not every 46-year-old com­e­dy still gets laughs, but Air­plane! seems only to get fun­nier with the decades. Some view­ers too young to have caught it in its the­atri­cal release even take the Ben­jamin­ian view of it as the kind of great work that cre­ates its own genre: the rapid-fire dead­pan joke machine, we could call it. But as the InCin­e­mat­ic video essay above reminds us, Air­plane! belongs, at its core, to that ven­er­a­ble comedic form of the par­o­dy. The key lies in its tit­u­lar excla­ma­tion point shared with Zero Hour!, a con­ven­tion­al Para­mount dis­as­ter movie from 1957 also about a dis­graced fight­er pilot forced to assume com­mand of an air­lin­er, albeit one with nary a laugh in its 81 min­utes.

Though it actu­al­ly runs six min­utes longer, Air­plane! feels much short­er, thanks in part to its mer­ci­less­ly con­stant vol­ley of humor. But unlike so many major par­o­dies of this cen­tu­ry, which feel like noth­ing so much as a tis­sue of rapid­ly expir­ing pop-cul­ture ref­er­ences, it also tells a gen­uine sto­ry with momen­tum of its own.

The film’s writer-direc­to­r­i­al trio of Jim Abra­hams, David Zuck­er, and Jer­ry Zuck­er under­stood that view­ers would come for the laughs, but as with Zero Hour! and the count­less oth­er dis­as­ter pic­tures at which Air­plane! pokes fun, they’d stay to find out what hap­pens. Hence the inspired choice to play the whole thing per­fect­ly straight, no mat­ter how groan-induc­ing the visu­al or ver­bal gags being deliv­ered.

All this works only because Abra­hams, Zuck­er, and Zuck­er cast the right actors: that is to say, non-fun­ny ones. At the time of Air­plane!‘s release, “most come­dies relied on actors to be fun­ny, but nobody had real­ly tried mak­ing a com­e­dy with­out come­di­ans before.” This meant that “the com­e­dy had to be there before the cam­era start­ed rolling,” so that the actors being seem­ing­ly unaware of the humor would only make it fun­nier. The per­son­i­fi­ca­tion of this method is, of course, Leslie Nielsen, who’d already put in a quar­ter-cen­tu­ry of dra­mat­ic per­for­mances (includ­ing in no less a sev­en­ties dis­as­ter spec­ta­cle than The Posei­don Adven­ture), but whose dead­pan turn as Dr. Rumack ele­vat­ed him into a kind of super­star­dom of the absurd. Whether a par­o­dy like Air­plane! would work if made today is dif­fi­cult to say, but it nev­er­the­less remains a les­son in sto­ry­telling for young film­mak­ers — comedic or oth­er­wise.

entries.title: The Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam Has Digitized 840,000 Works of Art, Including Great Works by Rembrandt and Vermeer
entries.summary: Art may seem inessential to those who make the big decisions in times of crisis. But it never seemed more necessary to artists working in the time of plague. So it was 366 years ago when Rembrandt painted a portrait of his son, Titus, in a monk’s robe in 1660. Eight years later, Titus was […]
entries.content:
Art may seem inessen­tial to those who make the big deci­sions in times of cri­sis. But it nev­er seemed more nec­es­sary to artists work­ing in the time of plague. So it was 366 years ago when Rem­brandt paint­ed a por­trait of his son, Titus, in a monk’s robe in 1660. Eight years lat­er, Titus was dead from plague, which had only a few years ear­li­er killed Hen­drick­je Stof­fels, Rembrandt’s for­mer house­keep­er and sec­ond wife, who helped raise Titus, Rembrandt’s only child to sur­vive into adult­hood.

These unimag­in­able loss­es “con­tributed to the tragedy and anguish we see in Rem­brandt’s late self-por­traits,” writes The Guardian’s Jonathan Jones. Dur­ing the plague, Rem­brandt also used his work as social cri­tique.

His etch­ing The Rat-Poi­son Ped­dler shows, “in a sense,” the Min­neapo­lis Insti­tute of Art’s Tom Rassieur tells the Star Tri­bune, “the guy who pur­ports to be helping—the exterminator—is prob­a­bly doing as much to spread the dis­ease as any­one else. That relates to [crit­i­cism] of our lead­er­ship today.” In his last years, Rem­brandt paint­ed self-por­traits of his iso­la­tion and grief that found a new audi­ence dur­ing the COVID lock­down.



Else­where in the Nether­lands, Rembrandt’s con­tem­po­rary Johannes Ver­meer was no stranger to the kind of social­ly iso­lat­ed world we found our­selves in dur­ing COVID. “His home­town of Delft was strick­en with plague sev­er­al times in the artist’s life­time. In 1635 and 1636 over 2,000 peo­ple died, and in the mid-1650s and mid-1660s hun­dreds more,” notes Breeze Bar­ring­ton at CNN. The qual­i­ties we most asso­ciate with Vermeer’s work, the soli­tude and atten­tive pres­ence, were devel­oped dur­ing time spent in iso­la­tion.

“In this time of forced iso­la­tion,” Friso Lam­mertse, cura­tor of 17th-cen­tu­ry Dutch paint­ing at the Rijksmu­se­um in Ams­ter­dam, not­ed dur­ing the pan­dem­ic, Vermeer’s work “can point us at the fact that extreme beau­ty can be found just in our room.” The Rijksmu­se­um did­n’t just rec­om­mend art in the pan­demic’s state of alone­ness, but also dou­bled its col­lec­tion of free, high-res­o­lu­tion works online, by Rem­brandt, Ver­meer, and a host of oth­er artists who used art to cope with loss and lone­li­ness dur­ing the plagues of their times. The muse­um now offers 840,000 dig­i­tized images in total.

The muse­um promised to “bring the muse­um to you,” and it has deliv­ered not only with its exten­sive dig­i­tal col­lec­tion, free for down­load­ing, shar­ing and edit­ing with a free Rijksmu­se­um account, but also with infor­ma­tive series on its web­site. Art is essen­tial in the best and worst of times, when it shows us how to look close­ly at our­selves, our loved ones, and our sur­round­ings, and treat life with more care and atten­tion. Enter the Rijksmu­se­um online col­lec­tions here.

An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2021.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

Josh Jones is a writer and musi­cian based in Durham, NC.

entries.title: Discover the Ancient Roman Shorthand Writing System with 4,000 Symbols Commissioned by Cicero
entries.summary: You can still type a symbol originally invented for Cicero nearly 21 centuries ago — at least if you configure your keyboard properly. The character ⁊ appears in Unicode as U+204A, but is better known as the “Tironian et”: the “et” is Latin for “and,” and the “Tironian” comes from its creator, a man named […]
entries.content:
You can still type a sym­bol orig­i­nal­ly invent­ed for Cicero near­ly 21 cen­turies ago — at least if you con­fig­ure your key­board prop­er­ly.  The char­ac­ter ⁊ appears in Uni­code as U+204A, but is bet­ter known as the “Tiron­ian et”: the “et” is Latin for “and,” and the “Tiron­ian” comes from its cre­ator, a man named Tiro, or in full, Mar­cus Tul­lius Tiro. Tiro was­n’t a rel­a­tive of Mar­cus Tul­lius Cicero, as you might expect, but rather his one­time slave: after being eman­ci­pat­ed, he not only took on two of his for­mer mas­ter’s names, but also remained his sec­re­tary and con­fi­dant. It was in that capac­i­ty that, at Cicero’s request, he cre­at­ed the sys­tem since known as Tiron­ian notes.

Though now cred­it­ed as “the father of stenog­ra­phy,” Tiro did­n’t invent short­hand itself. Like so many devel­op­ments in ancient Roman civ­i­liza­tion, Hel­lenic inspi­ra­tion was involved: no soon­er did Cicero learn of the exis­tence of Greek short­hand sys­tems, so the sto­ry goes, than he asked Tiro to come up with one for Latin. It’s pos­si­ble that he did so as ear­ly as 75 BC, when Cicero was assigned to Sici­ly and need­ed to encode his com­mu­ni­ca­tions, espe­cial­ly those hav­ing to do with the cor­rup­tion of local offi­cials. Back in Rome, it became use­ful indeed for rapid­ly tran­scrib­ing onto wax-cov­ered tablets what the great ora­tor had to say, in sit­u­a­tions rang­ing from every­day deal­ings in the Forum to — as record­ed by Plutarch — denounc­ing Cati­line’s con­spir­a­cy to over­throw the Roman Repub­lic.

Tiro cre­at­ed about 4,000 sym­bols to stand in for syl­la­bles, words, and oth­er ele­ments of lan­guage, and oth­er of the sys­tem’s users, includ­ing Seneca, lat­er brought the num­ber up to 5,000. But “as Rome declined, so did short­hand,” writes Ani­ta Kre­itz­man at the Nation­al Court Reporters Asso­ci­a­tion. “The Emper­or Jus­tin­ian, in the sixth cen­tu­ry, con­temp­tu­ous­ly for­bade its use.” Yet Tiron­ian notes sur­vived, espe­cial­ly among the anno­ta­tors of man­u­scripts, expand­ing and merg­ing with oth­er sys­tems to con­tain 14,000 signs dur­ing the Car­olin­gian dynasty. Alas, “Holy Roman Emper­or Fred­er­ick II (1212–1250) con­sid­ered the use of short­hand sym­bols ‘dia­bol­i­cal’ and ‘ordered the destruc­tion of all short­hand char­ac­ters.’ As a result, short­hand quick­ly became a lost art.”

There­upon came the Dark Ages in which “learn­ing and short­hand seemed to no longer exist.” Leave it to court reporters to equate abbre­vi­a­tion with civ­i­liza­tion. Yet the asso­ci­a­tion is hard­ly spu­ri­ous, and can’t be acci­den­tal that its revival began in late six­teenth-cen­tu­ry Lon­don, when the world’s trans­for­ma­tion over the sub­se­quent cen­turies was get­ting into motion. Many short­hand sys­tems have risen and fall­en since, and the dig­i­tal tech­nolo­gies of recent decades have made the whole prac­tice super­flu­ous for most of us here in the twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry. Yet we can still have ⁊, thanks to inad­ver­tent preser­va­tion by the medieval Irish script and Gael­ic type that use it as an amper­sand. It may not have the same func­tion in Eng­lish, or even the Romance lan­guages, but typ­ing no oth­er sym­bol could make us feel quite so Ciceron­ian.

Relat­ed con­tent:

entries.title: When the US Mail Was Delivered Underground at 35 MPH Through a Network of Pneumatic Tubes (1893–1953)
entries.summary: Twenty years ago, United States senator Ted Stevens drew long-lasting online ridicule by describing the internet as “a series of tubes.” While some commentators noted that the analogy wasn’t quite as outlandish as it seemed, most reacted with nothing more than amused bafflement. Where had Stevens come up with that image? Given that he was […]
entries.content:
Twen­ty years ago, Unit­ed States sen­a­tor Ted Stevens drew long-last­ing online ridicule by describ­ing the inter­net as “a series of tubes.” While some com­men­ta­tors not­ed that the anal­o­gy was­n’t quite as out­landish as it seemed, most react­ed with noth­ing more than amused baf­fle­ment. Where had Stevens come up with that image? Giv­en that he was born in 1923, per­haps he was draw­ing on mem­o­ries of a tech­no­log­i­cal won­der of his child­hood: the under­ground pneu­mat­ic sys­tems through which mail was deliv­ered in major Amer­i­can cities from the eigh­teen-nineties until the ear­ly nine­teen-fifties, whose sto­ry is told in the It’s His­to­ry video above.

Such series of tubes entered ser­vice in Lon­don, Paris, and Berlin in the mid-nine­teenth cen­tu­ry. In 1893, Philadel­phia became the first Amer­i­can city to get one, thanks to the advo­ca­cy of tech­no­log­i­cal­ly mind­ed depart­ment store mag­nate-turned-Post­mas­ter Gen­er­al John Wana­mak­er. At the inau­gu­ra­tion, writes Hid­den City’s Har­ry Kyr­i­akodis, Wana­mak­er “placed a Bible wrapped in an Amer­i­can flag into a can­is­ter that went fly­ing (under­ground) to the Cen­tral Post Office with a loud ‘whish’.” Philadel­phi­a’s net­work expand­ed apace, even­tu­al­ly includ­ing near­ly twen­ty miles of tun­nels, and “New York City, Boston, Chica­go, and St. Louis adopt­ed sim­i­lar deliv­ery sys­tems by 1898, all oper­at­ed by the Post Office Depart­ment.”

Oper­at­ed at a seri­ous loss, that is: when the U.S. got involved in World War I, the Post Office sus­pend­ed pneu­mat­ic ser­vice to con­serve resources. Only in the twen­ties did the tubes start whish­ing again in parts of New York and Boston, whose high vol­umes of mail could poten­tial­ly jus­ti­fy the oper­a­tion. In fact, the sheer amount of mail even­tu­al­ly got to be too much for the steel cap­sules and the cast-iron tun­nels through which com­pressed air pushed them. As retired U.S. Postal Inspec­tor Robert A. Cohen explains it in his his­to­ry of these sys­tems, “It takes a cer­tain amount of time for a gal­lon of liq­uid to trav­el through a fun­nel. Two gal­lons take twice as long to pass through. The val­ue of the Pneu­mat­ic Tube Ser­vice decreased as mail vol­ume increased.”

The pro­lif­er­a­tion of auto­mo­biles and the expan­sion of their sup­port­ing infra­struc­ture dealt an even more seri­ous blow: after World War II, deliv­er­ing mail on the roads had clear­ly become more effi­cient than doing it under­ground. Some “rock­e­teers,” as the sys­tem’s oper­a­tors were called, stuck it out until Decem­ber 12, 1953, when pneu­mat­ic mail ser­vice was offi­cial­ly sus­pend­ed all across the coun­try.

This marked the end of an era, espe­cial­ly for the rock­e­teers said to have used the net­work to sur­rep­ti­tious­ly receive orders from their favorite sand­wich shops. Remem­ber­ing Ted Stevens’ noto­ri­ous remark, it’s tempt­ing to describe the series of tubes that were pneu­mat­ic mail deliv­ery sys­tems as an ear­ly ver­sion of the inter­net — and even more so it was already get­ting peo­ple hooked on food deliv­ery.

]

Relat­ed Con­tent:

entries.title: One of the Best Preserved Ancient Manuscripts of The Iliad Is Now Digitized: See the “Bankes Homer” Manuscript in High Resolution (Circa 150 C.E.)
entries.summary: Each time I sit through the end credits of a film, I think about how weird auteur theory is—that a work of cinema can be primarily thought of as the singular vision of the director. Typical examples come from artier fare than the usual Hollywood blockbuster in which crews of thousands of stuntpeople, special effects […]
entries.content:
Each time I sit through the end cred­its of a film, I think about how weird auteur the­o­ry is—that a work of cin­e­ma can be pri­mar­i­ly thought of as the sin­gu­lar vision of the direc­tor. Typ­i­cal exam­ples come from arti­er fare than the usu­al Hol­ly­wood block­buster in which crews of thou­sands of stunt­peo­ple, spe­cial effects tech­ni­cians, and ani­ma­tors (and sev­er­al dozen “pro­duc­ers”) make essen­tial con­tri­bu­tions. In the case of, say, Wes Ander­son or David Lynch—or ear­li­er direc­tors like Godard or Kubrick—one can’t deny the evi­dence of a sin­gu­lar mind at work. Even so, we tend to ele­vate direc­tors to the sta­tus of god­like arti­fi­cers, sur­round­ed by a few angel­ic helpers behind the cam­era and a few star actors in front of it. Every­one else is an extra, includ­ing, very often, the actu­al writ­ers of a film.

Of course, the notion of the auteur comes from the gen­er­al the­o­ry of author­ship that iden­ti­fies lit­er­ary works as the prod­uct of a sin­gle intel­lect. French the­o­rists like Michel Fou­cault and Roland Barthes have cast sus­pi­cion on this idea. When it comes to writ­ing from the man­u­script age, hun­dreds or thou­sands of years old, it can be next to impos­si­ble to iden­ti­fy the author of a work.

Many an ancient work comes down to us as the prod­uct of “Anony­mous.” In the case of the major Greek epics, The Odyssey and The Ili­ad, we have a name, Homer, that most clas­sics schol­ars treat as a con­ve­nient place­hold­er. As a Uni­ver­si­ty of Cincin­nati clas­sics site not­ed, “Homer” could stand for “a group of poets whose works on the theme of Troy were col­lect­ed.”

Though writ­ten ref­er­ences to Homer date back to the 6th cen­tu­ry B.C., giv­ing cre­dence to the his­tor­i­cal exis­tence of the leg­endary blind poet, he might have been more direc­tor than author, bring­ing togeth­er into a coher­ent whole the labor of hun­dreds of dif­fer­ent sto­ry­tellers. For his­to­ri­an Adam Nicol­son, author of Why Homer Mat­ters, “it’s a mis­take to think of Homer as a per­son. Homer is an ‘it.’ A tra­di­tion. An entire cul­ture com­ing up with ever more refined and ever more under­stand­ing ways of telling sto­ries that are impor­tant to it. Homer is essen­tial­ly shared.” The nar­ra­tive poet­ry attrib­uted to Homer, Nicol­son sug­gests, might go back a thou­sand years before the poet sup­pos­ed­ly put it to papyrus.

You can read this Nation­al Geo­graph­ic inter­view with Nicol­son (or buy his book) to fol­low the argu­ment. It isn’t par­tic­u­lar­ly original—as Daniel Mendel­sohn writes at The New York­er, “the dom­i­nant ortho­doxy” for over a hun­dred years “has been that The Ili­ad evolved over cen­turies before final­ly being writ­ten down” some­time around 700 B.C. We have no man­u­scripts from that ear­ly peri­od, and no one knows how much the poem evolved through scrib­al errors in the trans­mis­sion from man­u­script to man­u­script over cen­turies. This is one of many ques­tions lit­er­ary his­to­ri­ans ask when they approach papyri like that at the top—an excerpt from the so-called “Bankes Homer,” the best-pre­served spec­i­men of a por­tion of The Ili­ad, con­tain­ing Book 24, lines 127–804, and dat­ing from cir­ca 150 C.E.

Pur­chased in Egypt in 1821 by Egyp­tol­o­gist William John Bankes, and acquired by an adven­tur­er named Gio­van­ni Finati on the island of Ele­phan­tine, the papyrus scroll, which you can see in full and in high res­o­lu­tion at the British Library site, was cre­at­ed like most oth­er “lit­er­ary papyri” for hun­dreds of years. As the British Library describes the process:

Pro­fes­sion­al scribes made copies from exem­plars at the request of clients, tran­scrib­ing by hand, word by word, let­ter by let­ter. Until around the 2nd cen­tu­ry CE these man­u­script books took the form of rolls com­posed of papyrus sheets past­ed one to the oth­er in suc­ces­sion, often over a con­sid­er­able length.

In addi­tion to the text itself, notes the site His­to­ry of Infor­ma­tion, the man­u­script con­tains “breath­ing marks and accents made by an ancient diorthotes or ‘cor­rec­tor’ to show cor­rect poet­ic pro­nun­ci­a­tion.” The ancient prac­tice of “cor­rect­ing” was a ped­a­gog­i­cal tech­nique used for train­ing stu­dents to prop­er­ly read the text. Like­ly for hun­dreds of years before there was a text, the poem would be com­mit­ted to mem­o­ry, and recit­ed by anony­mous bards all over the Greek-speak­ing world, prob­a­bly chang­ing in the telling to suit the tastes and bias­es of dif­fer­ent audi­ences. Who can say how many, if any, of those ancient bards bore the name “Homer”?

Again you can see the Bankes Homer in high res­o­lu­tion here (click the image to view in a larg­er for­mat).

Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2018.

Hear What Homer’s Odyssey Sound­ed Like When Sung in the Orig­i­nal Ancient Greek

entries.title: The Most Controversial Ancient Philosophy: Epicureanism
entries.summary: Over the years, you’ve probably heard at least a few people casually describe themselves as Epicureans. As used today, the label can refer to as little as enjoying the occasional expensive restaurant meal. The bar was a bit higher in the second century, as explained by ancient-history YouTuber Garrett Ryan in the new video above […]
entries.content:
Over the years, you’ve prob­a­bly heard at least a few peo­ple casu­al­ly describe them­selves as Epi­cure­ans. As used today, the label can refer to as lit­tle as enjoy­ing the occa­sion­al expen­sive restau­rant meal. The bar was a bit high­er in the sec­ond cen­tu­ry, as explained by ancient-his­to­ry YouTu­ber Gar­rett Ryan in the new video above from his chan­nel Told in Stone. But there is, at least, one major aspect of the orig­i­nal doc­trine laid out by Epi­cu­rus (341–270 BC) with which most any of his self-styled fol­low­ers in our time would agree: that plea­sure is the great­est good. Whether they would fol­low that premise all the way to the con­clu­sions Epi­cu­rus did is anoth­er mat­ter.

For that ancient Greek philoso­pher, Ryan explains, “hap­pi­ness was the sole legit­i­mate goal of human exis­tence. The essence of hap­pi­ness is free­dom from anx­i­ety. Since the great­est source of men­tal dis­tur­bance is fear about death and the after­life, it is nec­es­sary to under­stand the true nature of the uni­verse.”

There­after come the prin­ci­ples about atoms drift­ing through the infi­nite void, a sub­ject of less inter­est to many twen­ty-first cen­tu­ry “Epi­cure­ans” than the mechan­ics of the Williams-Sono­ma rewards pro­gram. Still, they would do well to learn at least one rel­e­vant Greek term: atarax­ia, or the “tran­quil­i­ty that comes from being suf­fi­cient in one­self.”

Achiev­ing atarax­ia is not a mat­ter of mere­ly indulging the sens­es. Rather, “all sources of unnec­es­sary men­tal dis­tur­bance should be removed.” That means no pol­i­tics and prob­a­bly no mar­riage, though friend­ship is accept­able. Though fair­ly ascetic in its orig­i­nal form, Epi­cure­anism drew quite a few high-pro­file Romans as adher­ents — and as detrac­tors. No less a fig­ure than Cicero, for exam­ple, attacked both its oppo­si­tion to tra­di­tion­al Roman reli­gion and, per­haps pre­dictably, its iso­la­tion from pub­lic life. Plutarch went so far as to write anti-Epi­cure­an trea­tis­es, includ­ing one titled “It Is Not Pos­si­ble to Live Plea­sur­ably Accord­ing to the Doc­trines of Epi­cu­rus.” That may or may not be true by our mod­ern stan­dards, but the ques­tion is worth con­tem­plat­ing over a good din­ner.

Relat­ed Con­tent:

Memen­to Mori: How Smil­ing Skele­tons Have Remind­ed Us to Live Ful­ly Since Ancient Times

entries.title: Watch Stewart Brand’s 6‑Part Series How Buildings Learn, With Music by Brian Eno
entries.summary: Stewart Brand came onto the cultural scene during the 1960s, helping to stage the Acid Tests made famous by Ken Kesey and the Merry Pranksters, and later launching the influential Whole Earth Catalog (something Steve Jobs described as “Google in paperback form, 35 years before Google came along”). He also vigorously campaigned in 1966 to have NASA release […]
entries.content:
Stew­art Brand came onto the cul­tur­al scene dur­ing the 1960s, help­ing to stage the Acid Tests made famous by Ken Kesey and the Mer­ry Pranksters, and lat­er launch­ing the influ­en­tial Whole Earth Cat­a­log (some­thing Steve Jobs described as “Google in paper­back form, 35 years before Google came along”). He also vig­or­ous­ly cam­paigned in 1966 to have NASA release a pho­to­graph show­ing the entire­ty of Earth from space—some­thing we take for grant­ed now, but fired human­i­ty’s imag­i­na­tion back then.

Dur­ing the 1970s and beyond, Brand found­ed CoEvo­lu­tion Quar­ter­ly, a suc­ces­sor to the Whole Earth Cat­a­log; the WELL (“Whole Earth ‘Lec­tron­ic Link”), “a pro­to­typ­i­cal, wide-rang­ing online com­mu­ni­ty for intel­li­gent, informed par­tic­i­pants the world over;” and even­tu­al­ly The Long Now Foun­da­tion, whose work we’ve high­light­ed here before. When not cre­at­ing new insti­tu­tions, he has poured his cre­ative ener­gies into books and films.

Above you can watch How Build­ings Learn, Brand’s six-part BBC TV series from 1997, which comes com­plete with music by Bri­an Eno. Based on his illus­trat­ed book shar­ing the same title, the TV series offers a cri­tique of mod­ernist approach­es to archi­tec­ture (think Buck­min­ster Fuller, Frank Gehry, and Le Cor­busier) and instead argues for “an organ­ic kind of build­ing, based on four walls, which is easy to change and expand and grow as the ide­al form of build­ing.”

Brand made the series avail­able on his YouTube chan­nel, with these words: “Any­body is wel­come to use any­thing from this series in any way they like… Hack away. Do cred­it the BBC, who put con­sid­er­able time and tal­ent into the project.” And he added the note­wor­thy foot­note: “this was one of the first tele­vi­sion pro­duc­tions made entire­ly in digital—shot dig­i­tal, edit­ed dig­i­tal.”

Find the first three parts above, and the remain­ing parts below:

You can find How Build­ings Learn added to our list of Free Doc­u­men­taries, a sub­set of our col­lec­tion, 4,000+ Free Movies Online: Great Clas­sics, Indies, Noir, West­erns, Doc­u­men­taries & More.

entries.title: How the Beatles Made their Most Acclaimed Album, Revolver, Released 60 Years Ago This Month
entries.summary: Among Beatles connoisseurs, it’s fair game to claim anything from Rubber Soul to Abbey Road as one’s favorite album. But even within that span of the catalog, a hierarchy of acclaim exists, and that hierarchy has been rearranged over the decades. The ecstatic reception of Sgt. Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band lasted at least a decade. […]
entries.content:
Among Bea­t­les con­nois­seurs, it’s fair game to claim any­thing from Rub­ber Soul to Abbey Road as one’s favorite album. But even with­in that span of the cat­a­log, a hier­ar­chy of acclaim exists, and that hier­ar­chy has been rearranged over the decades. The ecsta­t­ic recep­tion of Sgt. Pepper’s Lone­ly Hearts Club Band last­ed at least a decade. By the turn of the nine­teen-eight­ies, its imme­di­ate pre­de­ces­sor Revolver had joined it at the top spot of crit­i­cal regard; twen­ty years after that, Abbey Road had dis­placed Sgt. Pep­per. Now, a full 60 years after it first came out, Revolver is the sin­gle Bea­t­les album held in the high­est esteem — which, nat­u­ral­ly, makes it a seri­ous con­tender for the great­est album ever record­ed.

In his new video above, music YouTu­ber David Hart­ley explains what makes Revolver so beloved by recount­ing the his­to­ry of its pro­duc­tion. As in his pre­vi­ous Bea­t­les videos, he draws on the library of stu­dio out­takes that make audi­ble the evo­lu­tion of each song, as well as on con­tem­po­rary inter­views with the Bea­t­les and their col­lab­o­ra­tors.

Among his most illu­mi­nat­ing sources is engi­neer Geoff Emer­ick­’s mem­oir Here, There, and Every­where — titled, inci­den­tal­ly after one of the songs on this very album, the chal­lenge of whose record­ing he took on at just twen­ty years old. In the event, his youth proved an asset, grant­i­ng him as it did the will­ing­ness not just to exe­cute the Bea­t­les’ “far-out” son­ic ideas, but also to vio­late EMI Stu­dios’ poli­cies against exper­i­men­tal use of its hard­ware in the process.

Indeed, if it was pos­si­ble in 1966, it seems to have been tried in the mak­ing of Revolver. As Hart­ley reveals, “I’m Only Sleep­ing” once fea­tured a vibra­phone, “Yel­low Sub­ma­rine” once began with a spo­ken-word intro, and “And Your Bird Can Sing” once kept get­ting inter­rupt­ed by uncon­trol­lable and quite pos­si­bly sub­stance-induced laugh­ter. Nei­ther these nor any of the album’s oth­er now-famil­iar, much-scru­ti­nized songs took straight paths to their final forms. Into a run­time of only 35 min­utes, the Bea­t­les man­aged to put every­thing from “a chil­dren’s sin­ga­long song” to “a song com­plain­ing about all the mon­ey they were pay­ing in tax­es” to “a song about lone­li­ness” to “a song about lazi­ness” — while also trans­mit­ting the “great feel­ing of joy” for which their oeu­vre is known. Revolver’s place in the canon of albums is secure, but will it still be con­sid­ered the band’s best work on its 70th anniver­sary? Tomor­row, as they say, nev­er knows.

How the Bea­t­les Wrote Their Songs: From Ear­ly Demos to Final Record­ings
